newsitem.title: RUSSIA: RUSSIA KEEPS MARKETS AGOG OVER PGM EXPORT DELAYS.
newsitem.headline: RUSSIA KEEPS MARKETS AGOG OVER PGM EXPORT DELAYS.

text.p: Russia is keeping anxious world markets guessing over its reasons for delaying precious metal exports but industry officials here said on Tuesday that only ordinary red tape was to blame.

"The traditional bureaucratic foul-ups are the basic reason behind the break in Russian platinum group metal deliveries," said Yuri Kotlyar, first deputy director of the Norilsk Nickel group, Russia's biggest precious metals producer.

Kotlyar, quoted by the Kommersant Daily business newspaper, cited the recent cabinet reshuffle and dismantling of Roskomdragmet (the state committee for precious metals and stones, of which he was first deputy director before President Boris Yeltsin abolished it in August 1996) as behind the delays.

Prices for palladium, used in catalytic convertors, electronics and dentistry, hit a 17-year high last week, doubling this year to $240.00 an ounce. Sister metal platinum rose 20 percent last week alone to around $500.00 an ounce.

Both metals have risen over worries about Russia's delays in resuming deliveries of the white metals to Japan, the world's biggest buyer. Russia accounts for 60 percent of the world's palladium supply and one-fifth of platinum deliveries.

Industry officials denied a tug-of-war was ensuing between various entities for control over the exports, which bring Russia billions of dollars a year in hard currency, making the current rise in prices more than welcome to cash-hungry Moscow.
Norilsk Nickel has made no secret of its desire for a bigger cut from government exports of the metals. But a Norilsk spokesman said that that had played no role in the delays.

"It is our wish to make more money from the metals we produce, but it has no practical application yet," said Anatoly Komrakov. "We don't want to export directly -- but we do want a bigger commission from Russia's exports."

He said Almazjuvelirexport, the state precious metals export agency, was winning a commission from exports which should in part, he said, go to Norilsk. "We would like a commission of two percent of the world prices," he said.

Some traders suspect the Central Bank, which now manages the bulk of Russia's gold reserves, could be part of the delay. Sergei Kyshtymov, head of the Central Bank's directorate for precious metals operations, said he was aware of the hold-ups in exports but said the bank had played no role in them.
"We deal with gold and silver; those other (white) metals are the prerogative of the government," he said.

Vladimir Rybkin, head of the Finance Ministry's precious metals and stones section, told Reuters earlier on Tuesday that the Foreign Trade Ministry should award an export licence to Almazjuvelirexport this week, a key step to resuming exports.
When asked if the procedure for granting licences had changed, and if that could be behind the delays, he said, "No."

But Yuri Boikin, deputy head of the Foreign Ministry's foreign economic relations department, told Reuters Almazjuvelirexport already held a general licence to carry out exports this year and that no additional licences were needed.
"They have a general licence to export the volumes the government has told them to for 1997, and when they do that is their issue," he said.
Russian-Japanese talks on precious metals exports are usually held in December, with exports starting the next month for the calendar year.

The size of Russia's precious metals stockpiles is one of Moscow's best-kept state secrets, and Russian officials decline to comment when asked to state how big reserves are or if stockpiles are dwindling, as many London traders suspect.
But officials have been reluctant to explain the delays.
The current situation was simply a combination circumstances and it in no way reflected the presence of any sort of policy to push prices up, Kotlyar told Kommersant.
Japanese traders expect Russian exports to resume later this month or next, but Almazjuvelirexport and other industry officials have declined to be pinned down on a date.
Refiner Johnson Matthey estimates Russian palladium exports last year at a record 4.6 million ounces, mostly from strategic state stockpiles, and platinum at 1.22 million ounces.
Komrakov said the government owed Norilsk 770 billion roubles ($134 million) for precious metals but that this was not a factor in the delays.
"We're regularly unloading output to the state," he said. "What happens then is not our concern. We're just the producers."
